Where you didn’t know you were inside a memory yet.

caption.text:
You are not behind in life. You are not late. You are not missing some secret timeline everyone else seems to understand. You are simply becoming.

The truth is, some of the most important transformations happen quietly. They happen in the moments nobody celebrates. In the boundaries you finally set. In the people you finally stop chasing. In the peace you choose over proving yourself. In the way you keep showing up for your life, even when you have no guarantee that things will work out.

Maybe this season hasn’t looked the way you hoped it would. Maybe there are still prayers unanswered, plans unfinished, and dreams that feel farther away than they did at the beginning of the year. But growth isn’t only found in arrival. Sometimes growth is found in the waiting. Sometimes it is found in trusting that what is meant for you is still finding its way to you.

One day, you’ll look back at this version of yourself with so much tenderness. You’ll realize that while you were worrying about how far you still had to go, you were already becoming the person you prayed to be.

If you needed a reminder today: the best chapters of your story do not belong to your past. They belong to your future.

“Pre-order ‘How To Stop Breaking Your Own Heart’ now — out June 24, 2024.
—
What does a better you look like?

I remember being asked this question in therapy, and honestly, it didn’t take me long to respond. It’s easy to envision the perfect version of ourselves, a reality in which we live in freedom, beyond the constraints of what we subject ourselves to daily. I listed a bunch of things I would implement into my days to make them feel more fulfilled and productive, including all the qualities I would possess in order to have the ability to achieve these things.

My therapist responded with questions about my value system and my commitments to myself; it quickly became apparent that I wasn’t operating at my best, or even enough, to put these things into practice and bring them into my actual reality.

So, what was the issue? My foundations. I was still operating from a place of lack, from a mindset where I struggled to believe in myself or acknowledge my value. We have been led to believe that imposter syndrome is an individual issue, that only weak-minded people experience, when in fact, each and every one of us struggles with it. The only difference is, some people acknowledge what’s being said internally and choose to push past it, while others unfortunately allow themselves to get sucked into the lies and succumb.

My therapist made a point. He told me, “Your foundations are your grounds, your earth, your mud, your beginning. How can you expect anything to flourish in bad soil? Our foundations have to be set at a standard before anything has the chance to grow. We need to focus on developing your soil first and worry about planting seeds later.”

In my book, I talk about my journey to returning home to myself, the ways in which I had to break cycles, and the routes I took to find my way back.

Thank you in advance to everyone who has supported my work and placed an order.

It’s currently available for pre-order worldwide.

caption.text:
By now, I’m convinced that your soul knows when a season is coming to an end.

I never thought I’d be starting over at 36.

Grief, sadness, and depression held me for 1,706 days.

Stagnation. Procrastination. Complete hibernation from the version of me I once knew.

And yet, in the midst of all of that, my life’s work still stayed at the centre of my mind; every morning and every night.

I poured my soul into 2025, and with intention, I did everything needed to reclaim my life.

I survived the lowest of lows, and to be honest, rock bottom was the most freedom I’ve ever experienced.

There’s no urgency, almost everyone has written you off, and essentially, it’s just you vs. you.

The silence is loud. You’re faced with the reality of who you’ve become, and all you have is time, time to fix it.

Through all of these experiences, I’ve gained a deeper insight into life and collected so much wisdom.

I am of service, and I have so much to share. My spirit feels 100 years old.

I spoke to my elder Millie last night. We’re both Scorpios. She’s turning 93 next week.

She laughed when I told her that I feel like my life is over and reminded me that she has 56 years on me.

She said, “Starting over is just an invitation to return to the root of who you’ve become.”

It’s nothing to be ashamed of. If anything, it’s the complete opposite. What a privilege it is to be able to start over.

We’ve been led to believe that starting over is synonymous with failure,
 and because of that, many of us carry such deep levels of shame that we’d rather stay in positions we’ve outgrown than embrace the vulnerability of rebuilding something new.

So yeah, chipped nails, dry lips still showing up.

To anyone reading this: life can be rebuilt after loss, after trauma, after convincing ourselves that we aren’t worthy of experiencing it to its fullest extent.

Even if we’ve strayed light-years away from where we’re meant to be, we still have the ability to return home to ourselves.

caption.text:
My mother’s last wishes were for me to care for her father, my grandfather, and to ensure he wasn’t alone when it was time for him to transition.

The villain of the family. The man I wrote about in the opening chapter of my book, “How to Stop Breaking Your Own Heart,” and later, where I share a story about forgiveness and my mother’s journey to reconnecting with her father. My first heartbreak. The source of pain for my family for over 60 years.

A request I never understood, but knowing my mum, she had her reasons. So, I continued to trust her judgment in the three years since she passed away and cared for my grandfather.

This weekend, I buried my grandfather, closed a chapter, and broke a generational curse. Amidst all of this, I realized my mother’s last lesson for me was to understand and experience, for myself, the importance of forgiveness.

During this three-year process, I had no choice but to put my mental health first, regardless of who that offended. Many advised me to walk away and abandon my mother’s last request, underestimating that I live by a code and that my loyalty stretches far beyond the grave for those I cherish.

Some say I’m stubborn because I cannot be bought, persuaded, or controlled. But I know deep down, if I’ve been called to do something, then I will honor that and move accordingly until it is done.

In my book, I spoke about my mum reclaiming her life at the age of 60. I managed to do it by 34. My children will never have to walk this path.

This is what breaking generational curses looks like, and who feels it knows it.

Thank you to everyone who was patient with me during these years. I’ve been operating at 10% of my potential for over a decade and still managed to build a community of 24 million people and become a Sunday Times Best Selling Author. I’m excited to see how life changes now that I can pour 100% of my energy back into myself — in honour of my Mum and the years she lost.

Give thanks for freedom. 🙂

I pray, that if my Grandfathers soul has the opportunity to experience this life again, I hope he chooses to live in peace instead of pain. He deserves to know what that feels like too.

🌻

caption.text:
✨Introduction✨

Welcome to my little corner on the internet. My name is Ron and this is my story. 

I left behind my life back home in 2017. Nothing was fundamentally wrong. But I was unhappy and I wanted my life to be more. I didn’t know what “more” meant, but I knew I wasn’t going to find it back home. So I had to leave. 

I skipped university and “the system” and made up my own path instead. 

At that time, everyone I knew wanted to travel but they also wanted to be “sensible”. I wanted both. I wanted to travel and experience life, but I also wanted to build a business and be more successful than everyone else while I travel. 

I didn’t know where to begin, but I knew what I needed was more exposure in order to figure it out. I saved up a bunch of money for university, and decided to use it to travel instead. 

I worked on my business and traveled full time at the same time. For the first 2 years, I mostly backpacked. I’ve worked backpacking jobs, I’ve worked for free in exchange for accommodation, I’d meet people on the road and travel with them together, and I’d work on my phone on the bunk bed of hostels. 

Everything was terribly chaotic and confusing. But I wasn’t unhappy anymore. Intuitively, I knew I was on the right path. I just had to keep going through it and I knew things would make sense eventually. 

Fast forward, it’s been almost 7 years. I started when I was 22. I am on my last year of twenties now. 

For the most part, I am still on the same path. I still want exposure to life, and I am still highly ambitious. I am not where I want to be yet, but I am no longer confused like I was in my early twenties.

I know what I want now. And I know that the “gap” between where I am and where I want to be is simply dedicated efforts in the right direction. I’m confident enough to know that if I keep trying, I will figure it out. 

Ultimately, what I want is simply a life I feel happy living in. Do things I love doing. Be with people I like being with.

My Instagram account is really just me trying to document my life as it happens. Live life and write about it. The good, the bad, the lessons learned, and the reflections. That’s all I’m trying to do here.

Missing them will try to convince you that you made a mistake. That maybe you should go back, that maybe you let go too soon, that maybe it could still work if you just tried one more time. But missing someone is not the same thing as being meant to be with them. It just means what you felt was real.

So if you’re thinking about going back, read this again. Let yourself feel it, but don’t let it lead you somewhere that already broke you. It’s okay to miss them. It’s okay to wish it had worked. But it’s also okay — and necessary — to keep choosing yourself anyway. 🖤

caption.text:
The strange thing about being alive is how quickly it starts to feel normal.

You wake up inside a body you didn’t build, answer to a name someone gave you, carry a face you’ve never seen directly, and move through a world full of people having lives as private and complicated as your own.

At first, facts like these feel like little glitches in reality. Interesting, unsettling, almost funny. The kind of thing you read and then immediately want to tell someone else.

But the deeper point is not that life is strange.

The deeper point is that we stop noticing.

The brain is built to turn miracles into background noise. It has to. If you were constantly aware of how improbable and temporary everything is, you’d never get anything done. You’d just stand in the kitchen staring at your hands.

So the mind simplifies. It makes the moon ordinary. It makes your body ordinary. It makes time ordinary. It makes other people ordinary. It makes today feel like just another day.

Then one small fact breaks through and reminds you where you actually are.

On a planet.
In a body.
Inside time.
Surrounded by strangers who are also entire worlds.
Made out of matter older than memory.
Living a life that will someday feel impossible to explain.

caption.text:
How to move on after losing your mother? Find something new to pour your love into. 
. 
That was the advice I received from my godmother. At the time, it felt impossible. But over the past 4years, I’ve been trying my best to find things to love, until I realised the first thing I needed to focus on was myself. 
.
Grief absolutely crippled me but being faced with the reality of how ugly family can be, really highlighted how much my mother protected me.
. 
I realised that I spent a whole lifetime breaking my own heart due to the ricochet of the treatment I received growing up which resulted in me treating myself the same way. I wanted to stop that pattern. I wanted to break those chains. So I decided to do the one thing they always told me not to do: share my story. 
.
I decided to put everything into a book and build a community of people who went through the same thing, to speak to them and let them know that even though people around you may have spent years trying to break your heart, and even though you may have normalised that behaviour and ended up breaking your own heart, you can still return home to yourself. 
.
Because there is a beautiful life out there, a life that needs to be lived, that you have a right to pursue. And the quicker you fix your broken heart, the quicker you get to enjoy this human experience.
.
I learned a lot about forgiveness. I learned how to filter my community. I learned how to walk away from people I never thought I would have to walk away from and still have peace in my heart. I learned how to handle my pain.
.
I learned how to love myself again and how much it takes. The routines, the new habits, the lifestyle changes, everything you have to rebuild when you lose your rock.
.
So, if anyone reading this has lost a parent, pour your love into something else. The love your parent(s) left behind for you has manifested into a seed. You need to bury it, take care of it, and allow that seed to grow. That’s how you keep them alive. 
.
My mother always used to say, “People only die when you stop talking about them” and 65k have read her name.
.
Thank you to everyone who brought a copy of my book and made this possible. 🌻

caption.text:
Marlon Brando was one of the most influential figures in film history — an actor who transformed Hollywood with a style of performance that felt raw, authentic, and deeply human.

Born in Omaha, Nebraska, in 1924, he grew up in a troubled household marked by instability and emotional hardship. Far removed from the fame that would later define him, Brando spent his early years searching for purpose and belonging.

Through determination and natural talent, he rose to prominence in the 1950s and became one of the most celebrated actors of his generation. His performances in films such as A Streetcar Named Desire, On the Waterfront, and The Godfather redefined screen acting, bringing an unprecedented level of realism and emotional depth to the cinema.

What made Brando different was the complexity behind the legend. He possessed immense charisma and commanded attention wherever he went, yet he often felt uneasy with fame and resisted many of Hollywood’s expectations. 

Behind the public image was a thoughtful and often conflicted man who cared deeply about social justice and used his influence to support causes he believed in.

Throughout his life, Brando experienced extraordinary success as well as profound personal struggles. He became the father of eleven children and endured both great joys and heartbreaking losses. The contradictions that shaped his life also contributed to the depth and vulnerability audiences saw in his work.

He died on July 1, 2004, at the age of 80, but his influence has never faded. Marlon Brando remains a symbol of cinematic excellence — not just because he was a great star, but because he changed the very language of acting.

Even today, his legacy can be found in countless performances inspired by his example: the courage to strip away artifice and reveal something truthful beneath.

Hedy Lamarr was one of the most fascinating figures of 20th-century Hollywood. Behind the glamour and elegance was a brilliant and inventive mind that longed to be recognized for more than her appearance.

Her personal life was often turbulent. She was married six times and had three children, but despite her fame and many relationships, she often struggled to find lasting happiness and understanding.

As she grew older, Lamarr withdrew from public life and lived much of her later years in privacy. When she died in 2000 at the age of 85, she left behind more than a legendary film career. She became a lasting symbol of beauty, intelligence, and the remarkable achievements that can exist behind a famous face.
